lessons.title: Making predictions
lessons.goal: Speculate about the future and express different degrees of certainty.

tip.title: Futur simple & degrees of certainty
tip.body: The futur simple makes predictions: Dans vingt ans, les voitures rouleront toutes seules. Grade how sure you are: sans doute (probably — not 'without doubt'!), sûrement, probablement, peut-être. Il est probable que takes the indicative (il est probable que ça changera), but il est possible que and il se peut que take the subjunctive (il se peut que ça change). Pronunciation: the -rai/-ra endings are short and clear; in je serai, one e usually drops in speech: je s'rai or j'se-rai.

lessons.title: Debating AI
lessons.goal: Discuss the benefits and risks of artificial intelligence and hedge your claims.

tip.title: Hedging your claims
tip.body: Soften strong claims with a priori (on the face of it — say a-pri-o-ri), dans une certaine mesure (to some extent) and the journalistic conditional for unconfirmed information: selon les experts, l'IA remplacerait des millions d'emplois (reportedly would replace). Note IA is said i-a, and données (data) is feminine plural: les données sont protégées.

phrases.n: To some extent, AI saves us time.

phrases.n: According to some experts, AI could replace millions of jobs.

phrases.t: Le problème, c'est que ces outils se trompent parfois avec beaucoup d'aplomb.

lessons.title: Life online
lessons.goal: Talk about screen time, apps and digital habits.

tip.title: Screens, apps & the right to disconnect
tip.body: Talk about habits with sans arrêt (non-stop), régulièrement and à peine (hardly). Many tech words are English in France (un smartphone, une appli, le wifi — said oui-fi), but there are French options too: un téléphone, un portable, une application. France even has a legal 'droit à la déconnexion' (since 2017), meant to protect employees from work emails outside working hours. Pronounce écran with a nasal an: é-cran.

lessons.title: Futur antérieur: what will have happened
lessons.goal: Say what will be done by a certain point, and guess about the past.

tip.title: Futur antérieur = auxiliary in the future + past participle
tip.body: Build it like the passé composé, but put avoir or être in the futur simple: j'aurai fini, elle sera partie. Use it for an action completed before a point in the future: D'ici 2040, on aura remplacé les voitures à essence. Unlike English, French uses it after quand, dès que and une fois que when that action will be finished first: Appelle-moi quand tu auras fini (when you have finished). It can also guess about the past: Il aura oublié son mot de passe (he must have forgotten). Agreement works as in the passé composé.

story.title: Detecting disease with AI
story.intro: A Paris radio host interviews a Montréal researcher whose team uses AI to help doctors read medical images.

lines.name: Claire
lines.t: Bonjour Geneviève. Votre équipe, à Montréal, développe une intelligence artificielle pour les hôpitaux. Concrètement, ça veut dire quoi ?
lines.n: Hello Geneviève. Your team in Montréal is developing an artificial intelligence for hospitals. In concrete terms, what does that mean?

lines.name: Geneviève
lines.t: Notre logiciel analyse des radiographies et signale aux médecins les images qui semblent anormales.
lines.n: Our software analyses X-rays and flags the images that look abnormal to the doctors.

lines.name: Claire
lines.t: Est-ce que les radiologues vont devenir inutiles ?
lines.n: Are radiologists going to become useless?

lines.name: Geneviève
lines.t: Bien au contraire. L'outil fait le premier tri, et le médecin garde toujours le dernier mot. Ça lui laisse plus de temps pour les cas difficiles.
lines.n: Quite the opposite. The tool does the first sorting, and the doctor always has the final say. It leaves them more time for the difficult cases.

lines.name: Claire
lines.t: Et les patients, comment ont-ils réagi ?
lines.n: And the patients, how did they react?

lines.name: Geneviève
lines.t: Au départ, beaucoup de gens étaient sceptiques. Ils avaient peur qu'une machine décide à leur place.
lines.n: At first, a lot of people were sceptical. They were afraid a machine would decide for them.

lines.name: Claire
lines.t: Et dans dix ans, où en serez-vous ?
lines.n: And in ten years, where will you be?

lines.name: Geneviève
lines.t: J'espère qu'on aura convaincu les hôpitaux de toute la francophonie. Mais on va y aller une étape à la fois !
lines.n: I hope we'll have convinced hospitals throughout the French-speaking world. But we'll take it one step at a time!

lessons.title: Your view of the future

culture.title: Courriel, clavardage, divulgâcheur
culture.body: Québec is famous for creating French words for new technology. The Office québécois de la langue française (OQLF) promotes terms like courriel (email), clavarder (to chat online), égoportrait (selfie), mot-clic (hashtag) and divulgâcheur (spoiler). Courriel is also officially recommended in France, yet many French people still say un mail, and spoiler or selfie are common in everyday speech. The Académie française publishes a dictionary and gives usage advice, but cannot force anyone to follow it; in Québec, the Charter of the French language makes French mandatory in many areas — on commercial signs, for example, French must be predominant.
